strengths: Introduces a novel benchmark with two underexplored tracks for mobile GUI agents: proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution, addressing a gap in user-oriented agent evaluation.

Provides a large-scale longitudinal dataset of 21,437 episodes from 95 users across 506 apps, collected in real daily-life settings with rich contextual information (user profile, time, location, historical intents/actions).
Comprehensive experimental evaluation includes generalist MLLMs, GUI-specific agents, human study, fine-tuning baselines, difficulty analyses, and out-of-domain generalization tests.
Includes useful ablation studies on the contribution of screenshots, historical intents, contextual information, and probability-based intent prediction, supporting the benchmark design.
The proposed personalized metric is partially validated via a user study showing positive correlation with subjective user ratings.
The paper is clearly written, well-structured, and discusses ethical considerations, broader impacts, and limitations.
weaknesses: Reproducibility resources are incomplete in the manuscript: code and data links are missing/blank in the abstract, reproducibility statement, and Appendix A.4, which severely limits benchmark adoption and verification.

The personalized task execution test set is small (200 episodes), and success is checked manually; the proposed Sim2 metric (S_I / S_II) is an unbounded ratio that is not fully principled, despite partial validation.
The data is collected exclusively in mainland China from Chinese apps; generalization to other languages, regions, and app ecosystems is unclear and acknowledged as a limitation.
Benchmark reproduction is challenging because it relies on physical Android phones, ADB, and Chinese third-party apps rather than a publicly available emulator or containerized environment.
There is no mention of IRB/ethics approval, despite collecting sensitive user profiles and screen traces; data-sharing plans are unclear given privacy risks.
Human evaluation is limited: proactive task suggestion uses 20 annotators on 400 episodes, while personalized execution lacks a human success-rate comparison and relies on a small user-rating study.
Main proactive results use zero current screenshots, an extreme setting that may underrepresent practical agent performance, though the paper later varies screenshots.
The fine-tuned model does not surpass the best GUI-specific model on personalized success rate, so claims about 'good results' should be more carefully qualified.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale longitudinal mobile GUI dataset (20K episodes, 95 users, 506 apps) with rich user-related context (profile, time, location, historical intents/actions) and two novel evaluation tracks: proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution.
The paper formulates the two new tasks and provides initial baselines across generalist MLLMs, GUI-control agents, and a human study, which can motivate future work.
The data collection captures real daily phone usage rather than simulator-based annotations, and includes accessibility trees and action sequences useful for GUI agent research.
Fine-tuning experiments show that even small models can improve on some metrics when trained on the collected data, suggesting the dataset has potential value.
weaknesses: The proactive task suggestion task is under-specified and potentially ill-posed: in the main setup the agent receives zero current screenshots and must guess a free-form user intent from profile, time, location, and history. The low human ceiling (30.3% on a subset) suggests that exact-intent prediction is highly ambiguous, making the benchmark's central task difficult to interpret and potentially not measuring a well-defined capability.

Evaluation metrics are insufficiently validated. SR1 and Sim1 rely on an LLM judge and embedding/Levenshtein similarity, with no inter-rater reliability or sensitivity analysis. Sim2 (ratio of same-user to different-user action similarity) is unstable, can exceed 1, is not directly tied to task success, and may reward action sequences that mimic a user without completing the task. The user study for Sim2 is small (200 episodes, 4 models) and lacks statistical testing.

Data splits and leakage are unclear. The reported split sizes (16,000 + 4,411 + 1,000 + 200) exceed the stated total of 21,437, the two test sets partially overlap, and the validation-set construction is not described. Train/test users overlap, which is intended for personalization but makes generalization claims weaker; out-of-domain tests are very small (99–126 episodes).

Generalizability is limited: all 95 users are from mainland China and mainly use Chinese apps, so the benchmark's cultural, linguistic, and UI coverage is narrow. The paper acknowledges this but does not provide sufficient evidence that the tasks or metrics transfer to other regions/languages.

Experimental evidence for personalization is weak. The best fine-tuned model still substantially trails UI-TARS-1.5-7B on SR2 (15.5% vs. 38.5%), and improvements in Sim2 are small and not validated against human judgments at scale. There is no human performance baseline for personalized task execution, so it is unclear whether the models are meaningfully personalized.

Ethical/privacy risks are substantial and not fully resolved. The dataset collects continuous screenshots, accessibility trees, location, time, user profiles (including address, age, sex, marital status), and app traces. The anonymization strategy may not prevent re-identification; the paper acknowledges this only as a limitation, and the release of such data raises serious privacy concerns for a top-tier venue.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code/data are open-source but the provided URL is missing or anonymized, and it is unclear whether the dataset can be legally/ethically released. Key details for reproducing prompts, accessibility-tree processing, and human evaluation protocols are omitted or relegated to an appendix.

Presentation has inconsistencies: split numbers do not add up, some references and table formatting are sloppy (e.g., Reimers & Grzybowski vs. Reimers & Gurevych), and the relationship between the two tracks and practical agent deployment is not deeply analyzed.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely benchmark for proactive and personalized mobile LLM agents, with two clearly defined tracks and formalizations.

Collects large-scale, longitudinal, real-world mobile interaction data (21,437 episodes, 95 users, 506 apps) with rich user context such as user profile, time, location, historical intents, and historical actions, distinguishing it from prior datasets.
Provides comprehensive experiments: generalist MLLMs, GUI-specific agents, human study, fine-tuning, ablations, out-of-domain generalization, and cost analysis.
Human study and fine-tuning results demonstrate a significant gap between existing agents and humans, and show the value of user-oriented training for proactive/personalized capabilities.
Ethical and privacy measures are discussed, including anonymization, manual/automatic privacy checks, and data collection safeguards.
weaknesses: Data diversity is limited to mainland China and Chinese apps/users, which may limit generalizability to other regions, languages, and app ecosystems despite the limitation being acknowledged.

Personalized task execution evaluation relies on manual success checking and a nonstandard Sim2 ratio; human validation is small-scale, so stronger automated and larger-scale validation would improve confidence in the personalization metric.

The main proactive task suggestion setting uses zero current screenshots, which may be overly challenging and not fully reflect the intended proactive scenario, although ablations with screenshots are provided.

Dataset and code availability is not fully clear in the manuscript (the appendix data release link is missing/placeholder), and residual privacy/re-identification risks remain for sensitive UI traces even after anonymization.
Fine-tuning experiments are limited to a single 7B model with LoRA and two data scales; more model architectures and tuning strategies would strengthen the empirical conclusions.
